title: What would you simplify if the system had only 1% of the expected traffic?
description: Learn to distinguish architecture built for scale from architecture built for the current need, and explain which components you would remove, consolidate, or downgrade.

data.text: This question tests whether you optimize for the problem you have today or the problem you hope to have tomorrow. A senior engineer designs for the present while keeping future growth possible, but does not pay today for scale that is not needed yet.
What you might remove or downgrade

data.title: Common simplifications
items: Collapse microservices back into a modular monolith
Remove the CDN and serve assets directly
Disable auto-scaling and run a fixed number of instances
Replace Redis with in-memory caching or even omit caching
Remove message queues and process work synchronously
Downgrade database replicas to a single writer node

data.text: Not everything should be removed. Boundaries that protect correctness, security, and developer velocity often remain valuable even at low scale.

items: Module boundaries within a monolith—they keep the codebase maintainable
Authentication and authorization—security does not scale down
Structured logging and basic alerting—you still need to debug failures
Database migrations and schema versioning—data correctness matters at any scale

data.title: Avoid premature optimization
data.text: The best time to add caching, sharding, or microservices is when you have real evidence that the current architecture is the bottleneck, not when you anticipate future growth.

data.title: Simplifying a startup deployment
data.content: A startup runs Kubernetes with auto-scaling, a service mesh, and three read replicas. At 1% traffic, they could run a single server, remove the service mesh, and use one database. They keep structured logging because debugging still matters, but they stop paying for infrastructure they do not need.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Optimize for current load, not hypothetical future scale
Keep boundaries that protect correctness and maintainability
Add complexity only when metrics prove it is necessary
